summary:
A Workplace Insight guide (sponsored/advisory in tone) arguing that UK businesses should actively review business health insurance rather than auto-renewing. It explains why premiums rise at renewal: medical inflation driven by drug costs, specialist fees, diagnostic technology and hospital facilities; the policy's own claims experience; age-related repricing as the workforce ages; and insurer portfolio repricing decisions unrelated to the individual policy, such as an insurer becoming more or less competitive in the SME market.

It then sets out a five-part renewal review. First, whether cover still fits the team, since headcount, age profile, benefit expectations and occupational risk profiles change, leaving cover either insufficient or padded with unused benefits. Second, whether the premium is competitive, which requires a like-for-like market comparison across multiple insurers accounting for hospital networks, excess levels, outpatient limits and added-value services. Third, whether cover level and structure remain appropriate, given that product tiers shift and mental health provision, virtual GP access and cancer care pathways have evolved significantly. Fourth, whether the underwriting basis is still right: under moratorium underwriting, employees on the scheme two or more years may have had exclusions lifted, and a growing business may now qualify for medical history disregarded underwriting. Any change of underwriting basis takes effect at renewal, not mid-year. Fifth, whether the insurer performs well on claims, judged by process simplicity, assessment and payment speed, and network accessibility, with published ABI claims data offering a comparison baseline.

The piece closes (text truncated) on switching insurers: a legitimate outcome of review, but new underwriting terms apply as if the scheme were brand new, with the moratorium look-back period recalculated from the new start date, potentially reinstating exclusions previously lifted.

Core message: treat renewal as an active decision, brokered and benchmarked, not an annual formality.
